title: Biology Photosynthesis Knowledge Base
summary: Comprehensive extraction of examinable knowledge regarding photosynthesis, including equations, locations, light-dependent and light-independent reactions, limiting factors, uses of glucose, and common misconceptions.

knowledge.text: Overall equation for photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2, using light energy absorbed by chlorophyll.
Thylakoid membranes are stacked into grana and hold chlorophyll.
The fluid around the thylakoid membranes is the stroma.
Light-dependent reaction (thylakoid membranes): light excites electrons in chlorophyll (photosystems II and I).
Photolysis splits water into H+ ions, electrons, and oxygen, with oxygen released as a by-product.
Electron transport chain pumps H+ and drives ATP synthase to make ATP (photophosphorylation).
NADP is reduced to NADPH during the light-dependent reaction.
Light-independent reaction / Calvin cycle (stroma): enzyme RuBisCO fixes CO2 onto RuBP (5C) making two GP (3C).
GP is reduced to TP (triose phosphate) using ATP and NADPH in the Calvin cycle.
Some TP makes glucose and other organic molecules, while most regenerates RuBP using ATP.
Limiting factors of photosynthesis include light intensity, CO2 concentration, and temperature.
Temperature affects enzymes in photosynthesis; temperatures that are too high denature the enzymes.
The factor in shortest supply limits the rate of photosynthesis.
Uses of glucose produced in plants: respiration, starch for storage, cellulose for cell walls, sucrose for transport, and amino acids/proteins with nitrates.
Common misconception: plants also respire all the time.
Common misconception: oxygen comes from water, not CO2.
Common misconception: the Calvin cycle does not need light directly but needs products of the light-dependent reaction.

intro.text: You turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen using light energy absorbed by chlorophyll.
You explore chloroplasts containing thylakoid membranes stacked into grana holding chlorophyll, surrounded by the fluid stroma.
You power the light-dependent reaction in thylakoids and the light-independent Calvin cycle in the stroma.
You see how light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, temperature, and shortage dictate the rate.
You utilize produced glucose for respiration, starch storage, cellulose walls, sucrose transport, and amino acids.

sequence.title: Photosynthesis Flow
sequence.instructions: Jump through the correct stages in order!

steps.label: Light hits chlorophyll
steps.detail: Light excites electrons in chlorophyll within photosystems II and I on thylakoid membranes.

steps.label: Water photolysis
steps.detail: Photolysis splits water into H+ ions, electrons, and oxygen, releasing oxygen as a by-product.

steps.label: Electron transport chain
steps.detail: The electron transport chain pumps H+ and drives ATP synthase to make ATP via photophosphorylation.

steps.label: NADP reduction
steps.detail: NADP is reduced to NADPH during the light-dependent reaction.

steps.label: Carbon fixation
steps.detail: In the stroma, enzyme RuBisCO fixes CO2 onto RuBP making two GP.

steps.label: GP reduction
steps.detail: GP is reduced to triose phosphate using ATP and NADPH in the Calvin cycle.

steps.label: RuBP regeneration
steps.detail: Some triose phosphate makes glucose while most regenerates RuBP using ATP.

clues.label: Enzyme Heat
clues.claim: High temperatures denature enzymes in photosynthesis.
clues.why: Temperature affects enzymes, and temperatures that are too high denature them.

clues.label: Night Respiration
clues.claim: Plants only respire when it is dark.
clues.why: Plants also respire all the time as a common fact.

clues.label: Oxygen Source
clues.claim: Oxygen comes from splitting carbon dioxide.
clues.why: Oxygen comes from water during photolysis, not CO2.

clues.label: Calvin Light Need
clues.claim: The Calvin cycle needs direct light to function.
clues.why: The Calvin cycle does not need light directly, but needs products of the light-dependent reaction.

clues.label: Limiting Shortage
clues.claim: The factor in shortest supply sets the rate.
clues.why: The factor in shortest supply limits the rate of photosynthesis.
